blocks.x: MATH 157 · Algebra 11

Until now we focused on differentiation — finding the rate of change of a function. Integration reverses the process: given the derivative (gradient function), we find the original function. This module builds the rules, the techniques, and the real-world applications of integration.

3basic rules — Power, Constant, and Sum/Difference 4types of partial fractions (linear, quadratic, repeated, improper) 6real-world applications — area, average value, surplus, curves, DEs, partial derivatives
By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Find indefinite and definite integrals using the Power Rule, Constant Rule, and Sum/Difference Rule, and evaluate definite integrals over a closed interval [a,b].
2Integrate trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic forms, and apply integration by substitution and by partial fractions (Types I–IV) to integrate more complex rational functions.

3Apply integration to real problems — the average value of a function, area under a curve, area between two curves, finding the equation of a curve from its gradient function, and consumers'/producers' surplus in economics.

4Solve separable differential equations for general and particular solutions, and compute first-order partial derivatives of functions of two variables, interpreting them in applied (marginal) contexts.

blocks.x: Key definitions
Indefinite integral If F′(x) = f(x), then ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + c, where c is the constant of integration and F(x) is the antiderivative of f(x).

Definite integral
The definite integral of f(x) from a to b is ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> f(x)dx = [F(x)]<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> = F(b) − F(a), whenever F′(x) = f(x).
Rational function Any function of the form P(x)/Q(x), where P(x) and Q(x) are polynomials and Q(x) ≠ 0. It is proper if deg P < deg Q, and improper otherwise.

Separable differential equation
An equation of the form dy/dx = f(x)·g(y), which can be rearranged so all x-terms are on one side and all y-terms on the other, then integrated on both sides.

Partial derivative
For z = f(x,y), ∂f/∂x is found by differentiating with respect to x while treating y as a constant; ∂f/∂y is found by differentiating with respect to y while treating x as a constant.
Fundamentals→ Techniques→ Applications→ DEs & Partial Derivatives
Reversing differentiation
Integration finds the original function F(x) when its derivative f(x) is given. This section covers the three foundational rules, then definite integrals.
Notation In ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + c: ∫ is the integral sign, f(x) is the integrand, F(x) is the integral of f(x), c is the constant of integration, and dx tells us the variable of integration.
The Power Rule
For any real number n, where n ≠ −1: ∫x<sup>n</sup>dx = 1n+1x<sup>n+1</sup> + c
Compute ∫x&sup8; dx and ∫x⁻⁵ dx.

items: 1For ∫x&sup8;dx, apply the Power Rule with n = 8, so n+1 = 9.∫x&sup8;dx = x⁹/9 + c
2For ∫x⁻⁵dx, apply the rule with n = −5, so n+1 = −4.∫x⁻⁵dx = x⁻⁴/(−4) + c = −¼x⁻⁴ + c

blocks.x: Answer: x⁹/9 + c and −¼x⁻⁴ + c
Compute ∫√x dx.

items: 1Rewrite the surd as a fractional power: √x = x^(1/2), so n = 1/2, n+1 = 3/2.∫x^(1/2)dx = x^(3/2) / (3/2) + c
2Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal.= ⅔x^(3/2) + c

blocks.x: Answer: ⅔x^(3/2) + c
The Constant Rule
If k is any constant: ∫k dx = k∫dx = kx + c
Evaluate ∫(2x − 5)dx.

items: 1Integrate 2x using the Power Rule (n=1) and −5 using the Constant Rule.∫2x dx = 2·(x²/2) = x²; ∫−5 dx = −5x
2Combine both results and add a single constant of integration.x² − 5x + c

blocks.x: Answer: ∫(2x − 5)dx = x² − 5x + c
Sum and Difference Rule
For integrable functions f(x) and g(x): ∫(f(x) ± g(x))dx = ∫f(x)dx ± ∫g(x)dx
Find ∫(x² + 1/x² + √x)dx.

items: 1Split into three separate integrals and rewrite each term as a power of x.∫x²dx + ∫x⁻²dx + ∫x^(1/2)dx
2Apply the Power Rule to each term.= x³/3 + x⁻&sup9;/(−1) + ⅔x^(3/2)
3Simplify and combine into one constant of integration.= ⅓x³ − 1/x + ⅔x^(3/2) + c

blocks.x: Answer: ⅓x³ − 1/x + ⅔x√x + c
Definite Integrals

Definite integral Integrals containing an arbitrary constant c are called indefinite, since their precise value cannot be determined. A definite integral has limits of integration a and b: ∫ab f(x)dx = [F(x)]ab = F(b) − F(a).
Evaluate ∫<sub>1</sub><sup>3</sup>(3x² + 2x + 4)dx.

items: 1Find the antiderivative F(x) term by term.F(x) = x³ + x² + 4x
2Evaluate F at the upper limit, x = 3.F(3) = 27 + 9 + 12 = 48
3Evaluate F at the lower limit, x = 1.F(1) = 1 + 1 + 4 = 6
4Subtract: F(b) − F(a).48 − 6 = 42

blocks.x: Answer: ∫<sub>1</sub><sup>3</sup>(3x²+2x+4)dx = 42
If ∫<sub>−1</sub><sup>a</sup> 2(x+2)dx = 15, a > 0, find a.

items: 1Find the antiderivative of the integrand.F(x) = x² + 4x
2Apply the Fundamental Theorem: F(a) − F(−1) = 15.(a²+4a) − (1−4) = 15
4Factorise and solve, keeping only a > 0.(a+6)(a−2) = 0 ⇒ a = 2

blocks.x: Answer: a = 2
Evaluate the following:

items: ∫(x¹⁵³ + 5)dx
∫<sub>−2</sub><sup>2</sup>(x³ − x² + 1)dx
∫<sub>−2</sub><sup>2</sup>(x²−2)(2x−1)dx

blocks.x: Tip: expand any product of factors first, then integrate term by term using the three rules above.
Beyond the power rule

Not every integrand is a simple power of x. This section covers the standard trigonometric integrals, changing variables by substitution, integrals that yield logarithms/exponentials, and resolving rational functions into partial fractions first.
Standard trigonometric integrals
Integration by Substitution
Functions are not always presented in a directly integrable form. Substitution rewrites the integrand in terms of a new variable u so the Power Rule can be applied.
Evaluate ∫3x(4x²+3)⁵ dx.

items: 1Let u equal the inner function, then find du/dx.u = 4x²+3 ⇒ du/dx = 8x ⇒ du = 8x dx
2Rearrange to express 3x dx in terms of du, since we have 3x dx (not 8x dx) in the integral.x dx = du/8 ⇒ 3x dx = 3du/8
3Substitute u and 3du/8 into the integral.∫u⁵·(3/8)du = 3/8 ∫u⁵ du
4Integrate using the Power Rule, then substitute u back.= 3/8 · u⁶/6 + c = 1/16 (4x²+3)⁶ + c

blocks.x: Answer: ∫3x(4x²+3)⁵dx = (1/16)(4x²+3)⁶ + c
Evaluate ∫x√(1−x²) dx.

items: 1Let u = 1−x², so du/dx = −2x, i.e. x dx = −du/2.u = 1−x², x dx = −½du
2Substitute, rewriting √u as u^(1/2).∫u^(1/2)·(−½)du = −½∫u^(1/2)du
3Integrate using the Power Rule and substitute u back.= −½ · ⅔u^(3/2) + c = −⅓(1−x²)^(3/2) + c

blocks.x: Answer: −⅓(1−x²)^(3/2) + c
Integrals that yield Logarithmic and Exponential Functions

Logarithmic form
Since d/dx[ln(f(x))] = f′(x)/f(x), we get ∫f′(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + c. In particular, ∫1/x dx = ln|x| + c (the n = −1 case the Power Rule cannot handle).

Exponential form
Since d/dx(e<sup>x</sup>) = e<sup>x</sup>: ∫e<sup>x</sup>dx = e<sup>x</sup> + c, and more generally ∫e<sup>kx</sup>dx = (1/k)e<sup>kx</sup> + c.
Compute ∫1/(2x+3) dx and ∫2x/(3x²−2) dx.

items: 1For the first integral, the numerator (1) is not quite f′(x)=2, so introduce a compensating factor of ½.∫1/(2x+3)dx = ½∫2/(2x+3)dx = ½ln|2x+3| + c
2For the second, notice the numerator 2x IS the derivative of the denominator 3x²−2 up to a constant: d/dx(3x²−2)=6x, so scale by 1/3.∫2x/(3x²−2)dx = ⅓∫6x/(3x²−2)dx = ⅓ln|3x²−2| + c

blocks.x: Answers: ½ln|2x+3| + c and ⅓ln|3x²−2| + c
Evaluate ∫(2x+1)e^(2x²+2x) dx.

items: 1Let u = 2x²+2x (the exponent). Then du/dx = 4x+2 = 2(2x+1).du = 2(2x+1)dx ⇒ (2x+1)dx = du/2
2Substitute into the integral.∫e<sup>u</sup>·(½)du = ½∫e<sup>u</sup>du
3Integrate and substitute back.= ½e<sup>u</sup> + c = ½e^(2x²+2x) + c

blocks.x: Answer: ½e^(2x²+2x) + c
Integration by Partial Fractions
A rational function may be resolved (split) into a sum of simpler fractions, each of which is easy to integrate — usually into logarithms. There are four standard types, based on the denominator.
Type I — Linear factors
Denominator is a product of distinct linear factors, e.g. (x+3)(x−3). Each factor gets a constant-over-linear fraction: A/(x+3) + B/(x−3).
Type II — Quadratic factor
Denominator has an irreducible quadratic factor, e.g. (x+2)(x²+1). That factor gets a linear-over-quadratic fraction: A/(x+2) + (Bx+C)/(x²+1).
Type III — Repeated factor
A linear factor repeats, e.g. (x+2)(x−1)². The repeated factor gets one term for every power up to its multiplicity: A/(x+2)+B/(x−1)+C/(x−1)².
Type IV — Improper fraction
Degree of numerator ≥ degree of denominator. Divide first (polynomial long division) to get a whole part plus a proper remainder fraction, then resolve the remainder as above.
Type I: Express 6/[(x+3)(x−3)] as a partial fraction.

items: 1Write the fraction as a sum of unknowns A and B over each linear factor.6/[(x+3)(x−3)] = A/(x+3) + B/(x−3)
2Multiply both sides by (x+3)(x−3) to clear denominators.6 = A(x−3) + B(x+3)
3Substitute x = 3 (kills the A term) to find B, then x = −3 (kills the B term) to find A.x=3: 6=6B ⇒ B=1. x=−3: 6=−6A ⇒ A=−1

blocks.x: Type II: Resolve (11−4x−x²)/[(x+2)(x²+1)] into partial fractions.

items: 1Set up the fraction with a constant A over the linear factor and a linear (Bx+C) over the quadratic factor.= A/(x+2) + (Bx+C)/(x²+1)
2Clear denominators.11−4x−x² = A(x²+1) + (Bx+C)(x+2)
3Substitute x = −2 to isolate A.11+8−4 = A(5) ⇒ 15=5A ⇒ A=3
4Compare coefficients of x² and the constant term to find B and C.x²: −1=A+B ⇒ B=−4. const: 11=A+2C ⇒ C=4

blocks.x: Type III: Express 1/[(x+2)(x−1)²] as a partial fraction.

items: 1The repeated factor (x−1)² needs two terms: one over (x−1) and one over (x−1)².= A/(x+2) + B/(x−1) + C/(x−1)²
2Clear denominators.1 = A(x−1)² + B(x+2)(x−1) + C(x+2)
3Substitute x = 1 to isolate C, then x = −2 to isolate A.x=1: 1=3C ⇒ C=⅓. x=−2: 1=9A ⇒ A=&frac19;
4Compare coefficients of x² (A+B=0) to find B.B = −A = −&frac19;

blocks.x: Type IV: Resolve the improper fraction (x²+1)/(x²−3x+2) into partial fractions.

items: 1Degree of numerator equals degree of denominator, so divide first: x²+1 = 1·(x²−3x+2) + (3x−1).(x²+1)/(x²−3x+2) = 1 + (3x−1)/(x²−3x+2)
2Factor the denominator and resolve the proper remainder as Type I.x²−3x+2=(x−1)(x−2); (3x−1)/[(x−1)(x−2)] = A/(x−1)+B/(x−2)
3Solve for A and B by substitution (x=1 then x=2).x=1: 2=−A ⇒ A=−2. x=2: 5=B

blocks.x: Resolve into partial fractions, then integrate:

items: ∫5/[(x−2)(x+3)]dx — integrate each partial-fraction term as a logarithm.

blocks.x: Putting integration to work

Definite and indefinite integrals model geometric and economic quantities: the space under and between curves, the average of a continuously-varying quantity, and the gains enjoyed by consumers and producers in a market.
Average Value of a Function
The average/mean of n discrete numbers x₁,...,xn is x̄ = (x₁+...+xn)/n. For a continuous function f on [a,b], the average value is 1/(b−a) ∫ab f(x)dx.
Determine the average value of f(x) = x³−2x²−5x+1 on [−2,4].

items: 1Find the antiderivative F(x).F(x) = x⁴/4 − (2/3)x³ − (5/2)x² + x

blocks.x: Answer: Average value = 19/9 ≈ 2.11
Area Under a Curve
If y=f(x) is a curve, the area between the curve, the x-axis, and the lines x=a and x=b is A = ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> f(x)dx. The area is positive above the x-axis and negative below it.
Determine the area enclosed by the curve y = 2x+3, the x-axis, and the ordinates x=1 and x=4.

items: 1Set up the definite integral with the given limits.A = ∫<sub>1</sub><sup>4</sup>(2x+3)dx
2Find the antiderivative.F(x) = x²+3x

blocks.x: Answer: Area = 24 square units
The Area Between Two Curves
The area enclosed between y=f₁(x) and y=f₂(x) (with f₂ above f₁ on [a,b]) is A = ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> f₂(x)dx − ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> f₁(x)dx.
Find the area enclosed between y=x²+1 and y=7−x.

items: 1Find the intersection points by setting the curves equal.x²+1 = 7−x ⇒ x²+x−6=0 ⇒ (x+3)(x−2)=0 ⇒ x=−3, 2
2Since y=7−x lies above y=x²+1 on this interval, set up A = ∫[(7−x)−(x²+1)]dx from −3 to 2.A = ∫<sub>−3</sub><sup>2</sup>(6−x−x²)dx
3Integrate and evaluate at the limits.F(x)=6x−x²/2−x³/3; F(2)=22/3, F(−3)=−27/2
4Subtract F(−3) from F(2) and simplify.22/3 − (−27/2) = 44/6+81/6 = 125/6

blocks.x: Answer: Area = 125/6 ≈ 20.83 square units
Finding the Equation of a Curve from its Gradient
If dy/dx = h(x), then dy = h(x)dx, so y = ∫h(x)dx + c. A known point on the curve is substituted to solve for c, giving the particular equation.
A curve passes through (1,0). If the gradient function at any point P(x,y) is 3x²−1, find the equation of the curve.

items: 1Integrate the gradient function to get the general equation.y = ∫(3x²−1)dx = x³−x+c
2Substitute the known point (1,0) to find c.0 = 1−1+c ⇒ c=0

blocks.x: Answer: y = x³ − x
Consumers' and Producers' Surplus

Consumers' surplus (CS)
The benefit enjoyed by consumers willing to pay above the equilibrium price p₀ at quantity q₀: C.S = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>q₀</sup> f(q)dq − p₀q₀, where p=f(q) is the demand function.

Producers' surplus (PS)
The gain to producers willing to supply below p₀: P.S = p₀q₀ − ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>q₀</sup> f(q)dq, where p=f(q) is the supply function.
Demand: p=100−0.5q. Supply: p=10+q/10. Determine the consumers' surplus.

items: 1Find the equilibrium point by setting demand equal to supply.100−0.5q = 10+0.1q ⇒ 90=0.6q ⇒ q₀=150
2Find the equilibrium price p₀ by substituting q₀ back.p₀ = 100−0.5(150) = 25
3Integrate the demand function from 0 to q₀.∫<sub>0</sub><sup>150</sup>(100−0.5q)dq = [100q−0.25q²]₀¹⁵⁰ = 15000−5625=9375
4Subtract p₀q₀ from that integral.C.S = 9375 − (25)(150) = 9375−3750

blocks.x: Answer: Consumers' surplus = 5625

The demand function for a product q is p = 90/(q+2) and the supply equation is p = q+1. Find q₀ and p₀ at equilibrium (set the two expressions equal and solve), then use P.S = p₀q₀ − ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>q₀</sup>f(q)dq with the supply function f(q)=q+1.
Extensions
Two natural extensions of integration: solving equations that involve derivatives (differential equations), and differentiating functions of more than one variable.

Differential equation An equation containing an unknown function and one or more of its derivatives, e.g. dy/dx=xy. Its order is the order of the highest derivative present. A solution with an arbitrary constant is the general solution; using a given (initial) condition to find that constant gives a particular solution.

Separable differential equation A form dy/dx = f(x)·g(y), or dy/dx = f(x)/g(y) with g(y)≠0, where all x-terms can be moved to one side and all y-terms to the other. The method of solving it is called separation of variables.
Find the general solution of dy/dx = xy.

items: 1Separate the variables: move all y-terms (including dy) to the left, all x-terms to the right.dy/y = x dx
2Integrate both sides.∫dy/y = ∫x dx ⇒ ln|y| = x²/2 + k
3Exponentiate both sides to solve for y, relabelling e<sup>k</sup> as a new constant c.y = e^(x²/2+k) = c·e^(x²/2)

blocks.x: Answer: y = c·e^(x²/2)
Determine the particular solution of dy/dx = 3xy given x=0, y=3.

items: 1Separate variables.dy/y = 3x dx
2Integrate both sides.ln|y| = (3/2)x² + k ⇒ y = c·e^((3/2)x²)
3Substitute the initial condition x=0, y=3 to find c.3 = c·e⁰ = c ⇒ c=3

blocks.x: Answer: y = 3e^((3/2)x²)
The StrikeNow Company's marginal cost is dC/dx = −0.02x+6, 0≤x≤300. Find the particular cost function if the cost of producing 10 units is 400.

items: 1Integrate the marginal cost with respect to x to get the general cost function.C(x) = ∫(−0.02x+6)dx = −0.01x²+6x+k

blocks.x: Answer: C(x) = −0.01x² + 6x + 341
Partial Differentiation

For a function of two independent variables z=f(x,y), the partial derivative with respect to x, written ∂f/∂x or fx, is found by differentiating with respect to x while treating y as a constant. Similarly, ∂f/∂y or fy treats x as a constant.
Determine f<sub>x</sub>(x,y) and f<sub>y</sub>(x,y) for f(x,y) = x²y + y³x − 2xy.

items: 1To find f<sub>x</sub>, treat y as a constant and differentiate each term with respect to x.f<sub>x</sub> = 2xy + y³ − 2y
2To find f<sub>y</sub>, treat x as a constant and differentiate each term with respect to y.f<sub>y</sub> = x² + 3y²x − 2x

blocks.x: Answer: f<sub>x</sub> = 2xy+y³−2y, f<sub>y</sub> = x²+3xy²−2x
Marginal Productivity & Marginal Revenue
For a Cobb-Douglas production function Q(L,K)=ALaKb, QL (the partial derivative w.r.t. labour L) gives the marginal productivity of labour, and QK gives the marginal productivity of capital.

A company sells two products with demand functions p₁=1200−18x−y (military boots) and p₂=523−1.5x−0.15y (life jackets), where x,y are units sold per month. Find the revenue function R(x,y)=xp₁+yp₂, then R<sub>x</sub>(x,y).

items: 1Multiply each price by its quantity and add.R(x,y) = x(1200−18x−y) + y(523−1.5x−0.15y)
2Expand.R(x,y) = 1200x−18x²−xy+523y−1.5xy−0.15y²
3Collect the xy terms, then differentiate with respect to x, treating y as constant, to get R<sub>x</sub>.R(x,y)=1200x−18x²−2.5xy+523y−0.15y²; R<sub>x</sub>=1200−36x−2.5y

blocks.x: Answer: R<sub>x</sub>(x,y) = 1200 − 36x − 2.5y (the approximate change in revenue per extra unit of boots sold)

items: Find the general solution of dy/dx = x²/y³.
Determine the particular solution of dy/dx = 12x given x=1, y=8.
For f(x,y) = 5x²−6y³, find f<sub>x</sub> and f<sub>y</sub>.
